Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
301 PM EDT Fri Jul 31 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 301 PM EDT Friday...

No significant changes were made.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 301 PM EDT Friday...

1. Seasonable weather will continue through tomorrow. Aside 
from a few showers through this evening, the period looks dry.

2. Unsettled, showery weather is expected Sunday into Monday as 
waves of low pressure pass near our region. Risk of impactful 
weather has decreased somewhat.

3. Daily chances of showers and potential for a few thunderstorms 
are expected mid to late next week as temperatures warm above seasonal 
averages.   

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 301 PM EDT Friday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Localized showers and a thunderstorm or two remain on 
track today and tomorrow, with typical summertime weather 
anticipated. Through the rest of today, narrow strips stretching 
from north-northwest to south-southeast of regionally higher 
instability will continue to support scattered showers. Coverage is 
relatively high in northeastern New York, particularly in southern 
Franklin and Essex counties, with more isolated showers near and 
just east of the Green Mountain spine. There are also some cells
west of Montreal moving towards the International Border that we
will be watching. Overall, the pattern supports showers 
potentially pulsing up to produce a rare instance of lightning 
but little sustained thunderstorm activity, and diminishing past
peak heating/by sunset. Temperatures tonight and tomorrow 
should be on the warm side but within 5 degrees of normal; lows 
will mainly be in the mid 50s to low 60s and highs in the upper 
70s to mid 80s.

Chances for showers and thunderstorms are very low tomorrow with 
limited instability (CAPE peaking near 500 J/kg) and upper level 
ridging moving across our region. A rare shower could occur over the 
mountains, but it looks like a dry day. Late in the day into the 
nighttime hours, we will begin to see some large scale ascent with 
some cyclonic flow aloft and a developing surface front that will be 
largely stationary just to our west (near Ottawa stretching 
southwestward towards Lake Erie).

KEY MESSAGE 2: Chances for showers will increase gradually from Sunday 
into Monday, although we are becoming more confident that this will 
not be a significant event. It appears deeper convection capable of 
producing flash flooding will be to our southeast, not lining up 
with the pooling moisture over northern New York on Sunday/Sunday 
night. The latest global ensemble run shows a lower potential for 
extreme rainfall, with the 90th percentile rainfall amounts below 
2". That being said, a combination of increasing low level heat and 
humidity and cooling aloft will yield enough CAPE for at least 
occasional heavy downpours but low chance of thunderstorms. The 
higher risk of an isolated storm would be out ahead of where the 
bulk of shower activity will be (such as from the Adirondacks into 
northernmost Vermont), and then possibly shifting into central 
Vermont on Monday depending on timing of the system's cold front 
passing through. 

The position of the upper level trough on Sunday across the central 
Great Lakes region and surface reflection tracking northeastward 
into the eastern Great Lakes through the day supports a preference 
for most of the precipitation to stream northeastward across 
northern New York and far northwestern Vermont with much of our area 
mostly dry until Sunday night. The latest run of the NAEFS shows the 
axis of greatest PWAT, with an ensemble mean greater than 1.75", 
across the St. Lawrence Valley Sunday evening, shifting into Vermont 
and diminishing in magnitude overnight. While the corridor of deep 
moisture supports efficient rainfall especially with any training of 
showers, at this time it appears the bulk of the heaviest rainfall 
is targeted towards southern Canada. The expected axis of persistent 
cloudiness and showers leads to high temperatures on Sunday forecast 
to be fairly similar to Saturday in Vermont while several degrees 
lower in much of northern New York. Per upper air temperature 
climatology, portions of eastern Vermont, especially southern areas, 
are favored to be hottest although nothing particularly extreme; 
highs in the upper 80s are possible. 

Rainfall amounts through Sunday night remain uncertain but currently 
favored to be highest in the St. Lawrence Valley, averaging about 
0.75" to 1", where a slight risk (>15% and < 40%) of excessive 
rainfall exists. To the east, average amounts of 0.3" to 0.5" are 
indicated in far northwestern Vermont southwestward across the 
Adirondacks region, 0.1" to 0.25" in the Champlain Valley and north 
central Vermont, and under 0.1" in eastern Vermont. While the latest 
QPF is fairly bullish in a deterministic sense on Monday in Vermont 
(indicating amounts in the 0.5" to 1" in much of central and eastern 
Vermont), trends towards a faster progression of the northern stream 
trough and associated influx of drier air aloft point to lesser, 
widespread rainfall. So while precipitation chances on Monday have 
as anticipated increased, heavy rain is looking unlikely. Instead, 
it is more likely to be a beneficial rainfall, as much of northern 
Vermont is running at least a little below normal on precipitation 
over the last month or so.

KEY MESSAGE 3: Mean 500mb ridging is expected to shift slowly eastward 
with a nearly 600dm high anchored off the mid-Atlantic states and its 
axis just east of Vermont. This position favors unsettled conditions 
with weak cyclonic curvature aloft and flow out of the west to 
southwest as well as increasing temperatures with a building low to 
mid level ridging. With absence of strong capping in the 850-700mb 
levels, heating may be self-limiting as dew points rise promoting the 
formation of instability showers and potentially a few terrain 
initiated thunderstorms. Still high temperatures in the mid/upper 80s 
will feel uncomfortable with heat indices possibly exceeding 90 
Thursday. Some models point to a passing trough Thursday as well, so 
diurnal instability and this trigger mechanism could combine to produce 
a few stronger variety thunderstorms in this scenario. However, timing 
and strength of the trough is suspect this far out and may not be 
coincident with maximum heating.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z FRIDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY/...
Through 18Z Saturday...Aside from a few showers in eastern
Vermont and near the Adirondacks, conditions will remain quiet
today. A stray shower may occur at EFK/MPV/SLK through 20Z with
best chances of occurrence at EFK where showers are ongoing. By
20Z the wave responsible will be shift southeastward drier air,
evident on water vapor imagery, working into the region.
Otherwise, the main forecast concern will be for overnight fog.
MPV and EFK are most likely to see IFR or lower CIG/VIS
restrictions given clearing skies and a solid radiational
cooling set up 02-14Z. SLK still appears likely to be affected 
by fog, but could have a lingering low/mid CIG that may delay 
onset of fog. 

Outlook...

Saturday Night: VFR. Slight chance SHRA.
Sunday: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Likely SHRA, Slight
chance TSRA.
Sunday Night: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. Definite
SHRA, Slight chance TSRA.
Monday: MVFR/IFR conditions possible. Chance SHRA, Chance TSRA.
Monday Night: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Slight chance
SHRA.
Tuesday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Tuesday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Wednesday: VFR. Slight chance SHRA, Slight chance TSRA.
